paper_title: DMAD: Distribution Matching as Adversarial Distillation for Fast Visual Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) trains a few-step student from the difference between separately estimated target and student scores, so it must keep an auxiliary diffusion model fitted to the student's evolving distribution at extra memory and computation cost. We introduce DMAD, Distribution Matching as Adversarial Distillation, which recasts distribution matching as classification and learns the required log-density ratios directly. Two discriminator heads on a shared backbone distinguish real data and teacher samples from the student's, and linear losses on their logits train the student without auxiliary score fitting. We prove that at the discriminator optimum these losses recover the distribution-matching gradient underlying DMD, through the classical identity linking discriminator logits to log-density ratios. We further introduce gap-based reweighting, which adapts teacher supervision across noise levels from the real-data head's empirical logit gap between real and teacher samples. DMAD reaches a Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) of 1.04 with one-step generation on ImageNet-64x64, 14.47 with four-step SDXL on COCO-10K, and a VBench total score of 85.15 with four-step Wan2.1-T2V-14B, the best values among the compared few-step methods and the multi-step teachers. On MiniMax-H3-33B, our four-step student achieves overall human preference rates of 79.1% over DMD2 and 84.6% over rCM for joint audio-video generation, excluding ties. Our code, models and demos are available at https://yzmblog.github.io/projects/DMAD.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Diffusion models generate high-quality images and videos [11, 29, 38, 40], but sampling requires many sequential denoising steps. Step distillation reduces this cost by training few-step generator from pretrained teacher. Existing approaches supervise the student along the teachers sampling trajectories [16, 31, 39] or match distributions [47, 48]. Distribution matching lets the student learn its own mapping from noise to samples while preserving the target distribution. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [48] trains the student on the difference between target and student scores. frozen teacher supplies the target score, while an auxiliary diffusion model, the critic, tracks the evolving student distribution. When the critic lags behind, its score estimate carries error and training destabilizes. DMD2 [47] mitigates this with two time-scale update rule (TTUR) that runs five critic updates 1 Figure 1 Samples of our four-step student distilled from MiniMax-H3. Zoom in for details. per student update. Stability improves, but the student score is still only approximated, and each student update costs five critic passes. Beyond the critic, DMD2 evaluates the teacher online during training, adding further memory and computation cost. Its denoising task also constrains the architecture of the discriminator. We introduce DMAD, Distribution Matching as Adversarial Distillation, which replaces separate score estimation with two classification tasks, one against teacher samples and one against real data. Two discriminator heads distinguish these targets from student samples, and linear losses on their logits drive the updates. At the discriminator optimum, this loss yields the distribution-matching gradient underlying DMD (Proposition 1). DMAD eliminates auxiliary score fitting. In our experiments, we use one discriminator update per student update. Freed from the denoising task, the discriminator can build on diffusion encoders or pretrained classification features. The teacher now only supplies samples, so we generate them once and cache them, removing online teacher evaluation from training. Errors in separately estimated scores can be large relative to their difference, which drives the student update. We examine this in controlled experiment on two nearby Gaussian mixtures with known gradients, holding the student distribution fixed and giving both estimators the same teacher pretraining and seed. Figure 2 compares DMDs score difference with our single-head logit gradient. In this setting, our estimate follows the ground-truth field more closely, with normalized mean squared error of 0.144, compared with 1.539 for DMD. Section B.2 gives the setup and the analytic gradients. DMAD draws on two targets, the teachers samples and real data, which play complementary roles. Previous methods, including DMD2 [47], SiDA [52], and SenseFlow [6], add adversarial supervision on top of scorebased objective. In contrast, our discriminator heads carry the distribution-matching gradient themselves. Each head compares student samples with one target, and linear loss on their logits trains the generator. The real-data head supplies supervision beyond the teachers sampled distribution. Teacher samples alone would bound the student by the teachers own fidelity; training against real data lifts that bound, and our students outperform their teachers on both ImageNet and COCO. Our ablations in Table 4 demonstrate the complementary roles of the two targets: removing the real-data head raises four-step FID from 14.47 to 21.37 on COCO-10K, while removing teacher supervision reduces semantic fidelity and visual quality, dropping VBench total score from 84.70 to 82.20 and semantic score from 79.55 to 75.36. The balance between the two targets can vary across noise levels. During training, the real-data head assigns different mean logits to real and teacher samples (Figure 7(a)). This gap varies across noise levels and depends on the current student and discriminator. We use it as an empirical signal for gap-based reweighting, assigning larger teacher weights to noise bands with lower gaps. This adaptive allocation improves performance for both image and video generation  (Table 4)  . Our contributions are: We introduce DMAD, distribution-matching distillation framework that jointly learns from teachergenerated samples and real data through two binary classification tasks, eliminating auxiliary score fitting and online teacher evaluation. We develop gap-based reweighting, which uses the real-data heads mean responses to teacher and real samples within each noise band to adapt the teachers supervision as training proceeds. DMAD achieves 1.04 FID with one-step generation on ImageNet-6464 and 14.47 with four-step SDXL on COCO-10K, where one step reaches 16.11. Fourstep Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and -14B reach VBench total scores of 84.70 and 85.15. These are the best values among the compared few-step methods and the multi-step teachers. On the 33B MiniMax-H3 [28], human raters prefer our four-step student to DMD2 in 79.1% and to rCM [51] in 84.6%, excluding ties. Figure 2 Gradient estimation on two Gaussian mixtures with fixed student. Our logit gradient more closely matches the ground-truth field than DMDs score difference.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Trajectory and consistency methods. Early work distills teacher either by regressing to its outputs [24, 27] or by progressively reducing the number of sampling steps [31]. PDD [36] extends this idea to video using multi-interval mean velocities. Consistency and flow-map methods impose consistency along common trajectory, either by mapping different states to the same endpoint or by relating states at different points on that trajectory [16, 37, 39]. sCM [22] extends consistency modeling to continuous time, while MeanFlow [7] enables one-step generation from scratch. These methods all constrain how the student follows particular trajectory. Distribution matching instead constrains the distribution of its outputs. Score-based distribution matching. Diff-Instruct [26], VSD [41], and DMD [48] optimize generator through score-based distribution matching. DMD uses the difference between target score and score fitted to the students evolving distribution. DMD2 [47] removes the regression loss and strengthens online critic training, while SenseFlow [6] improves stability for large flow-based models. SiD [53] and SGMD [43] derive alternative objectives from score identities and Fisher-based matching. DP-DMD [42] and PhasedDMD [5] distribute supervision across generation steps or noise intervals. rCM [51] combines score regularization with consistency training, AnyFlow [9] learns flow-map transitions for any-step video generation, and AMD [1] adapts distribution matching using reward proxies. These methods still rely on score estimation. FSFDMD [17] removes the auxiliary fake-score network but derives fake-score surrogate from the generators own flow map. Our method instead estimates no score and learns the required log-density ratio directly through classification. Adversarial distillation. Adversarial distillation typically trains discriminators against real images or videos [19, 20, 33], or uses intermediate teacher predictions as adversarial targets [18, 34]. D2O-F [49] finetunes pretrained diffusion model with projected discriminator. DMD2, SiDA [52], SenseFlow, and ADM [23] add adversarial supervision to score-based distribution-matching objective. DDO [50] connects likelihood ratios to an implicit discriminator, while -distill [44] uses density ratios to reweight score differences. Unlike these methods, we do not use adversarial training to supplement score-based objective. The discriminator logits themselves provide the distribution-matching gradient, eliminating student-score estimation. Separate heads match teacher samples and real data, with their balance adapted across noise levels.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: We reformulate DMDs score-estimation pipeline as joint classification-based matching to teacher samples and real data. Linear losses on two discriminator logits train the few-step student. The same real-data head also scores teacher samples, and the gap it leaves between them and real data adapts teacher supervision across noise levels. Figure 3 illustrates the pipeline for video distillation. Image distillation is the same, with only the discriminator heads adapted to the backbone (Section B).

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate DMAD on class-conditional image generation, text-to-image synthesis, and text-to-video synthesis. Following DMD2 [47], we distill EDM [14] for ImageNet-6464 [4] and SDXL [29] for zero-shot generation on 10K COCO 2014 prompts [21]. We use Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [10] to measure image quality and diversity, and CLIP score [30] to evaluate textimage alignment. For SDXL, we additionally report patch FID [3, 18] to assess high-resolution details, following DMD2. For video, we distill Wan2.1-T2V 1.3B and 14B [40] to four steps and evaluate them with VBench [12] on the same augmented prompt set as rCM [51]. We further distill MiniMax-H3 [28] to four steps and evaluate them in user study and AVGen-Bench [54]. Training and evaluation details are provided in Section B. More results are shown in our supplementary demo video. 6 Figure 4 Qualitative comparisons of our DMAD and baseline models on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B. Rows show the teacher, DMD2, sCM, rCM, and ours. Within each example, columns show frames 1, 28, 55, and 81 in order. All compared videos are generated using identical initial noise and text prompts. Prompts are abbreviated for presentation.

sections.title:
4.2 Main Results
Class-conditional image generation. Table 1 compares DMAD with recent baselines. Our one-step model
achieves an FID of 1.24, outperforming DMD2, including its longer-training variant, and SiDA trained directly
from the teacher. It also outperforms the EDM teacher with both ODE and SDE samplers. With a projected
discriminator following D2O-F [49], DMAD achieves an FID of 1.04, surpassing D2O-F and SiD2A, which is
initialized from a SiD-distilled generator. The advantage comes from our formulation: the discriminator itself
provides the distillation gradient, so discriminative representations directly guide generator training. DMD2,
in contrast, requires a critic that must be refitted continually to the student’s evolving distribution, five times
per student update.
sections.content: Text-to-image synthesis. We follow DMD2 [47] for both training data and evaluation. Our generators are trained by distilling SDXL [29] using 500K real images from LAION-Aesthetics [35] and corresponding teacher-generated samples, and evaluate on zero-shot COCO 2014 [21]. Our four-step generator achieves an FID of 14.47 and patch FID of 19.88  (Table 2)  , outperforming DMD2, SenseFlow [6], and the SDXL teacher on both metrics. With single forward pass, DMAD achieves an FID of 16.11 and CLIP score of 0.338, the best one-step FID and highest CLIP score among the compared models. Qualitative comparisons appear in Figure 8. Text-to-video synthesis. We distill Wan2.1-T2V 1.3B, 14B [40] and MiniMax-H3 [28] into four-step generators using real videos from UltraVideo [45] and corresponding videos generated by the teacher. sections.title:
4.3 Ablation Studies
We study four ablations in Table 4: removing the teacher head, removing the real head, disabling gap
reweighting with fixed loss weights, and replacing the linear generator loss with the non-saturating GAN loss.
Removing a head also removes its discriminator and generator losses. For removing the real head, we also
disable gap-based reweighting, which depends on the real-data head.
sections.content: Removing the real head causes the largest FID increase on ImageNet and SDXL in Table 4. The teacher-only curve in Figure 7(b) also stays above the full model and rises again after about 400K iterations. Removing the teacher instead slows the decrease in ImageNet FID. Although it gives the lowest SDXL FID, it also gives the worst patch FID and CLIP, and reduces the VBench semantic score by 4.19 points. Our combined adversarial objective improves ImageNet convergence and SDXL detail and text alignment over either target alone. Replacing the linear generator loss with the non-saturating loss slows the reduction in ImageNet FID. As shown in Figure 7(b), our model first records FID below 1.5 at 209K iterations, compared with 354K for the non-saturating variant. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented DMAD, reformulation of distribution matching distillation that jointly learns from teachergenerated samples and real data without auxiliary score fitting. Starting from DMDs score-difference update, DMAD trains the student through linear losses on two discriminator logits, which at the discriminator optimum recover the same distribution-matching gradient. Training requires no online teacher evaluation and uses one discriminator update per student update. We further use the real-data heads gap between real and teacher samples to adapt teacher supervision across noise levels. Experiments show improvements over the compared few-step methods and multi-step teachers in image FID and VBench total score. On MiniMax-H3, users prefer our four-step student over DMD2 and rCM, particularly in visual and audio quality. These results support discriminative learning as an effective approach to distribution matching distillation.

sections.title: AI use statement
sections.content: We used large language models to assist with polishing the writing, retrieving and discovering related literature, and drafting portions of the manuscript. The authors take responsibility for the final content of this work, including its claims, citations, and any text produced with the aid of these tools.

sections.title: Ethics statement
sections.content: This work develops efficient distillation methods for image and video generation. While faster generation can benefit creative applications and research, it can also lower the cost of producing misleading or harmful synthetic media. Distilled models may inherit biases and inappropriate generation behaviors from their teachers and training data. We encourage responsible use of these methods, with appropriate safeguards against impersonation, misinformation, and non-consensual content.

sections.title: Reproducibility statement
sections.content: Section 3 describes our method, and Appendix provides the theoretical derivation. The experimental setup and implementation details, including model architectures, training hyperparameters, and evaluation protocols, are provided in Section 4 and Appendix B. We will publicly release our training and evaluation code, dataset preparation and preprocessing scripts, and experiment configurations to facilitate independent reproduction and further research.

sections.title: B Implementation Details
sections.content: Training and evaluation configuration. We use AdamW with (β1, β2) = (0, 0.99) and one discriminator update per generator update. All reported models use generator EMA weights. ImageNet and SDXL use an EMA half-life of 106 generated images with ramp-up factor 0.05. Wan and MiniMax-H3 uses power-function EMA [15] with σrel = 0.1. For ImageNet-64 64, we train on 8 H100 GPUs with global batch size 384, learning rates ηG = ηD = 2 106, λT = λR = 0.003, and 570K iterations. For SDXL, we train on 8 H100 GPUs with global batch size 64, ηG = ηD = 5 107, λT = λR = 0.005, and 17K iterations. For Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, we train on 8 H100 GPUs with global batch size 8, ηG = ηD = 2 106, λT = λR = 1, and 17K iterations. For Wan2.1-T2V-14B, we train on 64 H100 GPUs with global batch size 8, ηG = ηD = 106, λT = λR = 1, and 19K iterations, using FSDP and context parallelism with groups of 8 GPUs. For evaluation, we follow the protocols of DMD2 [47] for ImageNet and SDXL, and rCM [51] for Wan2.1-T2V. For MiniMax-H3, we train on 8 H200 GPUs with global batch size 8 at resolution of 1344768 for 800 iterations, using ηG = ηD = 4105 and λT = λR = 1. Both the generator and the discriminator backbone use LoRA with rank and alpha set to 128. For evaluation, we follow the protocols of DMD2 [47] for ImageNet and SDXL, rCM [51] for Wan2.1-T2V and AVGen-Bench [54] for MiniMax-H3. For user study in MiniMax-H3, we conduct pairwise user study using 387 prompts from VideoGenEval [46]. For each prompt, we compare the audio-video output of DMAD with those of DMD2 and rCM, yielding 774 pairs. All models use four sampling steps. Pairs are presented as A/B comparisons with the left/right placement of DMAD balanced within each baseline. Each pair is evaluated by three annotators on five dimensions: prompt alignment, visual quality, motion quality, audio quality, and overall preference. For each dimension, annotators select A, B, or tie. This yields 2,322 pairwise evaluations. For each prompt and dimension, we aggregate the three judgments by majority vote, recording tie if all three judgments differ. Each baseline therefore has 387 prompt-level outcomes per dimension. We report the preference rate for DMAD as Nwin/(Nwin + Nloss) over these outcomes, excluding ties. For overall preference, the win/tie/loss counts are 204/129/54 against DMD2 and 247/95/45 against rCM, with tie rates of 33.3% and 24.5%, respectively. Discriminator architecture. The real and teacher heads share feature backbone. For ImageNet and SDXL, the diffusion discriminator uses pretrained U-Net encoder and middle block with two convolutional heads. Each head downsamples the features using 4 4 convolutions, group normalization, and SiLU, then predicts scalar logit. For the projected-discriminator variant on ImageNet, we follow D2O-F [49] and use frozen ImageNet-pretrained VGG16-BN and EfficientNet-Lite0 backbones with two trainable sets of multi-scale discriminator heads. For Wan, two MLP heads with SiLU activation operate on final-block tokens, and their logits are averaged over the video. For MiniMax-H3, final-block features undergo non-affine RMS normalization before entering two MLP heads, each consisting of two linear layers with SiLU activation between them. For noise-band reweighting, ImageNet uses six bands over Karras indices 20500, grouped by 100 indices, with the last containing only index 500 (σ 2.527), SDXL uses 100-timestep bands, Wan uses 10 equal-probability bands under its discriminator-time sampling distribution, and MiniMax-H3 uses ten equal-width bands in the base time variable over [0, 1]. We use τ = 0.5 for ImageNet and SDXL training and τ = 2 for Wan and MiniMax-H3. B.1 Training Speed and Memory Table 5 compares the online training cost of DMD2 and DMAD on NVIDIA H200 GPUs, with matched batch sizes and input shapes within each setting. ImageNet and Wan-14B use full-parameter training, while MiniMax-H3 uses rank-128 LoRA. We measure CUDA-synchronized update times after warm-up and peak allocated GPU memory. Time includes one generator update and its associated critic updates. Following the official DMD2 configuration, we use 5:1 critic-to-generator update ratio for DMD2, compared with 1:1 for DMAD. Evaluation and checkpointing are excluded. B.2 Toy Gradient Estimation Distributions. sections.title: D Additional Qualitative Results
sections.content: D.1 SDXL Comparisons Qualitative comparisons in Figure 8 show that DMAD produces more natural colors and textures and follows the prompts more closely, while some DMD2 and SenseFlow samples appear oversaturated. The tennis example highlights natural skin texture, while the bird example shows distinct wing structure and fine feather detail. In the bench example, only our model satisfies the instruction to exclude cats. It also generates exactly four people in the family portrait, whereas the teacher, DMD2, and SenseFlow include extra people. D.2 MiniMax-H3 Teaser Prompts We list the prompts for the six samples in Figure 1, ordered from left to right and top to bottom. 1. medium shot opens on seasoned, grey-bearded man in sunglasses and paisley shirt, Beside him, younger man in tank top. In the background, vibrant mural splashes across wall, hinting at an urban setting. Faint city murmurs and distant chatter drift in, accompanied by mellow, soulful hip-hop beat that adds contemplative yet grounded atmosphere. The older man speaks while the younger man turns toward him, laughs softly, shakes his head in amusement, and then looks back at the camera. The camera slowly pushes in. "The city always got story," the older man murmurs with slight nod. The younger man chuckles and replies, "Yeah, you always say that." 2. breathtaking, painterly 2D animated continuous visual narrative, rendered with the lush, vibrant, and slightly surreal, almost dreamlike, infused with the intricate, delicate detail of traditional Japanese 18 Figure 8 Quality comparison of DMAD with the SDXL teacher, DMD2 [47], and SenseFlow [6]. All distilled models use 4 sampling steps, while the teacher uses 50 sampling steps. Images in each row share the same text prompt and initial Gaussian noise. Our model produces more natural colors and realistic textures with better text alignment. (Zoom in for details.) woodblock prints (Ukiyo-e), follows young, adventurous, and kind-hearted girl (perhaps with bright, curious eyes and wearing simple, practical, beautifully patterned traditional Japanese farm attire) as she befriends colossal, gentle, ancient Forest Spirit. The Spirit is magnificent, awe-inspiring creature, its form harmonious blend of animal and plant perhaps with moss-covered, antler-like branches, fur like shimmering leaves that change color with its mood, and eyes like deep, tranquil forest pools. They meet in sun-dappled, sacred grove deep within an ancient, primeval forest, where impossibly tall, gnarled trees form living cathedral and tiny, glowing, friendly forest sprites (Kodama-like) peek from behind 19 mossy rocks and giant, fantastical mushrooms. The girl, initially awestruck, offers the massive Spirit small, carefully cultivated offering perhaps perfectly ripe persimmon or handful of wild berries her gesture one of pure, innocent respect and affection. The Forest Spirit responds with slow, gentle inclination of its massive head, its leafy fur rustling like thousand whispers, and perhaps causes shower of magical, luminous flower petals to drift down from the canopy, or tiny, new sapling to sprout at the girls feet. The animation captures the incredible, detailed textures of the forest, the Spirits majestic yet gentle presence, and the profound, unspoken emotional connection forming between the child and this ancient guardian of nature. The color palette is rich symphony of deep forest greens, earthy browns, vibrant floral hues, and the soft, magical glow of the sprites and the Spirits own subtle luminescence. This continuous, sweeping visual journey is celebration of the profound, often mystical, bond between humanity and nature, the innocence and courage of childhood, and the power of kindness and respect to bridge even the most fantastical of divides, an affectionate, visually intoxicating ode to ecological harmony and interspecies understanding. The only implied sounds are the gentle rustling of leaves, the distant calls of unseen forest birds, the girls soft, respectful breathing, the Spirits deep, resonant, almost inaudible hum, and soaring, emotionally resonant, orchestral score. 3. The video opens with medium, eye-level shot of beautiful woman with dark hair and warm brown eyes. She wears magnificent, high-fashion flamingo dress with layers of pink and fuchsia feathers, complemented by whimsical pink, heart-shaped sunglasses.
